title: Motivating the least confident students
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino, a science teacher, argues that the usual response to students who say they are bad at the subject or find lessons boring, which is to make lessons more fun, produced enjoyment but almost no learning in her own classroom. She now aims to show students that success in science is attainable, and builds that on four foundations: consistently enforced behaviour expectations, well-established routines, clear coherent explanations, and a culture of learning. Routines are defended against the charge that they make lessons mundane, since predictability tells a reluctant student that they can succeed at participating. The culture of learning rests on regular feedback, linked homework, deep questions and framing mistakes positively. She is candid that none of this produces instant motivation and that the results appear over weeks of consistency.
points: Fun games and activities gave Castelino enjoyable lessons with hardly any learning, so engagement-first motivation failed her least confident students.
Behaviour must be dealt with first and relentlessly, because nothing else works in a classroom with a negative atmosphere.
Predictable routines with a clear why, simple steps and a unique cue make every student, including the unmotivated, more able to succeed.
Motivation comes from students experiencing success, supported by clear explanations, regular feedback, linked homework and positive framing of mistakes.
Consistency is the hard part and results show over weeks, not instantly.
quotes: Of course, my students may have had a good time in lessons (mostly because they could play games and talk to their mates) but hardly any learning took place.

If the behaviour in your classroom is not perfect, then it doesn’t matter what else you try because it simply won’t work. Especially if you have that class. You know, the one in which the atmosphere is so negative that neither you nor the kids want to be there.

I know this because my classroom has been Classroom A for a long time. Since switching to Classroom B, I have seen the difference it has made to my students. This difference was not visible instantly but over weeks.
The mechanics of the lesson are now sorted. For students to truly feel successful and motivated, clear explanations are important.
A classroom culture in which students feel they can participate is great but is not enough to sustain motivation. We need to provide opportunities for continuous learning.
I have been doing this for years and while some students are quick to feel motivated, others are on their way but not quite there yet.
